confidence_flag: The SKILLS STRUCTURE and GRADE-BY-GRADE TOPIC PROGRESSION (sections marked strand_structure) are directly sourced from the official national syllabus document and are verified/reliable - the syllabus text even uses IsiNdebele as its worked example (e.g. 'Subject: IsiNdebele' in the sample scheme of work). isiNdebele is taught using this same national structure as ChiShona, in the learner's own language. The actual VOCABULARY/PHRASE content (sections marked strand_content) is standard, well-established isiNdebele language content grounded in general linguistic knowledge of the language (isiNdebele is closely related to isiZulu) - it was NOT extracted from the official textbook's specific word lists, so treat vocabulary choices as representative/standard rather than verbatim-official. Core grammar and vocabulary facts are accurate.

chunks.topic: Structure of the Indigenous Languages Syllabus
chunks.content: isiNdebele is taught under the national Indigenous Languages syllabus, which covers ECD A through Grade 7 as a single spiral curriculum: the same four skills (Listening/Observing, Speaking/Signing, Reading, Writing/Brailling) and broadly the same topics are covered at every grade, gaining in breadth and depth as learners progress. At the Infant level (ECD A - Grade 2), the learner's indigenous language (isiNdebele in Ndebele-speaking areas, mainly Matabeleland) serves as the medium of instruction across the whole curriculum, not just as a language subject. From Grade 3, it continues as a dedicated subject alongside English. The syllabus is explicitly designed to inculcate the values of Ubuntu, promoting and cherishing Zimbabwean identity.

At Junior level, isiNdebele is assessed through continuous assessment (30% of the final mark, covering drawing, speaking, written exercises, theory exercises, and research projects on culture and heritage) and summative assessment (70%). Summative assessment has two papers: Paper 1 (40 marks) consists of 40 multiple-choice questions covering register, aspects of culture, comprehension, language usage and language structure; Paper 2 (30 marks) has Section A (composition - candidates choose one from five questions) and Section B (comprehension and summary, 5 marks each).

Listening/Observing topics progress from Grade 3's sounds made by objects/animals/materials, word sounds, rhymes/jingles/riddles, dialogue, news/stories/folktales, instructions and times of day; through Grade 4-5's phonetic sounds, totems, sustained dialogue and stress/intonation work; to Grade 6-7's debates on cross-cutting themes, voice and mood in speech, and messages from different media. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to retell folktales, identify moral lessons from folktales, and demonstrate understanding by answering questions. Common activities include storytelling, retelling stories and news, drama, role play, memory games, and singing songs and rhymes to strengthen listening skills.
learning_activities: Listening to and retelling isiNdebele folktales (inganekwane), identifying the moral lesson
Playing sound and memory games with radios, percussion instruments and ICT tools
Listening to and discussing debates on cross-cutting themes in upper grades

chunks.content: Speaking/Signing topics progress from Grade 3's likes/dislikes, roles of self and family members, counting games, reciting rhymes and folktales; through Grade 4-6's totems, myths and taboos, heritage sites, natural resources, debates on cross-cutting themes, and appropriate registers/requests; to Grade 7's prepared and unprepared speeches, riddles/idioms/proverbs, common myths and legends, and figurative expressions. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to tell stories on emerging and cross-cutting themes, debate, dramatise, recite poems and rhymes, and retell folktales.
learning_activities: Reciting rhymes, jingles and riddles (izilibho) in isiNdebele
Debating cross-cutting themes using appropriate register
Presenting prepared and unprepared speeches by Grade 7

chunks.content: Reading topics progress from Grade 3's syllable sounds, words and sentences, news/stories/folktales, extensive reading, and simple graphs/maps/tables; through Grade 4-6's meanings of words from context, referencing skills, skimming and scanning, idioms/similes/proverbs/ideophones, and inferences; to Grade 7's modern and ancient ways of communication, and continued work on comprehension, intonation and enunciation. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to read a variety of materials, demonstrate understanding through answering questions, and comment on emerging and cross-cutting issues read.
learning_activities: Reading isiNdebele texts for comprehension and identifying idioms and proverbs (izaga)
Practising skimming and scanning skills on graphs, maps and tables in isiNdebele
Discussing modern and traditional ways of communication in Grade 7

chunks.content: Writing/Brailling topics progress from Grade 3's Nelson's script handwriting, punctuation, comprehension questions, creative writing, spelling and dictation, composition, and idioms/riddles/similes/proverbs; through Grade 4-6's poems and prose, summaries, business and friendly letters, telegrams, emails, blogs, essays with linking paragraphs, and information from graphs/pictures/tables; to Grade 7's continued essays, short stories, folktales, creative work, comprehension, summary, spelling, dictation and punctuation, plus ICT tools in writing throughout. By the end of the junior course, learners should be able to write creative works, write in appropriate register, and write with grammatical accuracy, correct spelling and appropriate punctuation. Note: the official syllabus's own sample scheme of work uses isiNdebele as its worked example subject, confirming punctuation, spelling, letter writing and creative writing are all explicitly covered.
learning_activities: Practising Nelson's script handwriting in isiNdebele from Grade 3
Writing formal and informal letters in isiNdebele by Grade 5-6
Composing essays, short stories and folktales with correct spelling and punctuation by Grade 7

chunks.content: Common isiNdebele greetings: 'Salibonani' (Hello, to a group/formal), 'Sabona' (Hello, to one person, informal), 'Livuke njani?' (How did you wake up? - a common morning greeting to a group), 'Uvuke njani?' (How did you wake up? - to one person), 'Ngivukile, wena unjani?' (I woke up well, and you?), 'Kulungile' (I am fine / it is fine). Time-of-day greetings: 'Livukenjani' is often used generally in the morning; 'Litshonile' can be used as an evening greeting. Farewells: 'Sala kuhle' (Stay well, said to the one remaining) / 'Hamba kuhle' (Go well, said to the one leaving). 'Ngiyabonga' means thank you; 'Ngiyaxolisa' means I am sorry.

isiNdebele numbers 1-10: kunye (1), kubili (2), kuthathu (3), kune (4), kuhlanu (5), isithupha (6), isikhombisa (7), isificaminwembili (8), isitshiyagalolunye (9), itshumi (10). Numbers 11-20 are formed as 'itshumi lanye' (ten and one, 11), 'itshumi lambili' (12), continuing to 'amatshumi amabili' (20, literally 'two tens'). As with ChiShona and other Bantu languages, isiNdebele numbers show grammatical agreement with the noun class of what is being counted, so the exact form used changes depending on the object counted.

Common isiNdebele family/kinship terms: 'Umama' (mother), 'Ubaba' (father), 'Umntwana' (child), 'Umnewethu' (older brother/sister of the same sex, used by a younger sibling), 'Umfowethu' (brother, referring to a male sibling), 'Udadewethu' (sister, referring to a female sibling), 'Ukhulu' (grandfather), 'Ugogo' (grandmother), 'Ubabekazi' (paternal aunt), 'Umalume' (maternal uncle). isiNdebele kinship terms, like those in ChiShona, often carry specific cultural roles and responsibilities within the extended family structure beyond their direct English translation.

chunks.topic: Days of the Week and Time (Insuku)
chunks.content: isiNdebele days of the week: uMvulo (Monday), uLesibili (Tuesday), uLesithathu (Wednesday), uLesine (Thursday), uLesihlanu (Friday), uMgqibelo (Saturday), iSonto (Sunday). Time-related vocabulary: 'Lamuhla' (today), 'Kusasa' (tomorrow), 'Izolo' (yesterday), 'Umnyaka' (year), 'Inyanga' (month), 'Iviki' (week, a loanword).

isiNdebele, like ChiShona and other Bantu/Nguni languages, organises nouns into noun classes marked by characteristic prefixes, which determine the agreement pattern for adjectives, verbs and pronouns. Common classes include: Class 1/2 (umu-/aba-, mostly people, e.g. 'umuntu' person / 'abantu' people), Class 3/4 (umu-/imi-, mostly plants and objects, e.g. 'umuthi' tree / 'imithi' trees), Class 5/6 (i-(li-)/ama-, e.g. 'ilizwi' word / 'amazwi' words), Class 7/8 (isi-/izi-, e.g. 'isihlalo' chair / 'izihlalo' chairs), and Class 9/10 (in-/izin-, often animals, e.g. 'inja' dog / 'izinja' dogs). isiNdebele is closely related to isiZulu and shares much of this Nguni noun-class system. Correct noun class is essential for subject-verb and adjective agreement in a sentence.

Common isiNdebele colour terms: 'Mhlophe' (white), 'Mnyama' (black), 'Bomvu' (red), 'Luhlaza' (green/blue - the word can cover both depending on context, a common feature in many Bantu languages), 'Phuzi' (yellow). Basic descriptive adjectives: 'Khulu' (big), 'Ncane' (small), 'Lide' (long/tall), 'Fitshane' (short), 'Kuhle' (good/nice), 'Kubi' (bad). As with nouns, adjectives take a prefix agreeing with the noun class of the thing being described.

Useful everyday isiNdebele phrases: 'Ngifuna amanzi' (I want water), 'Ngilambile' (I am hungry), 'Ngiya esikolo' (I am going to school), 'Ngubani ibizo lakho?' (What is your name?), 'Ibizo lami ngu...' (My name is...), 'Ngicela' (Please, literally 'I request'), 'Yebo' (Yes), 'Hatshi'/'Cha' (No), 'Ngikhona' (I am here/well), 'Kangizwisisi' (I don't understand).

Totems and clan praise names (izithakazelo) are an important feature of Ndebele culture, functioning as clan/family identifiers, often associated with an animal, natural object, or ancestral reference, and recited to show respect - especially to elders - as a form of greeting or acknowledgement of identity. They play a role in regulating social relationships, including marriage customs, and reinforce a sense of belonging and heritage within Ndebele society. The syllabus's Speaking/Listening strands reference totems from Grade 4 onward, building in depth through to Grade 7's inclusion of totems and their significance alongside heritage sites and natural resources.
